headline: Rust Crate Tampering launches Multi-Stage Info-Stealer Malware via build.rs
summary: This supply chain attack injects malicious dependencies into widely used Rust crates, activating info-stealing malware during the build process, targeting developer machines and CI/CD credentials.
details: A new supply chain attack is injecting multi-stage information-stealing malware into legitimate Rust crates. This malicious code is launched during the build process via build.rs without needing the target code to execute.
The attack is highly severe because it targets widely used crates and their dependencies, compromising developer machines and CI/CD credentials simply by Cargo resolving dependencies and building.
While 'Attack Attempt Observed' means suspicious activity was identified, code execution or data theft is not yet verified. Security teams should escalate their response based on further evidence.

Even organizations not directly using Rust can be affected through third-party vendors, open-source builds, and shared CI infrastructure. Security Operations Centers (SOCs) should monitor network traffic and child processes under build tools, not just executable distribution.
Developers who ran Rust builds during the affected period should immediately report their machines to their security team for investigation, rather than attempting to delete files themselves.
caption:
A critical supply chain attack is targeting Rust developers, injecting multi-stage info-stealer malware directly into legitimate crates during the build process.

While 'Attack Attempt Observed' means suspicious activity was identified, code execution or data theft is not yet verified. Security teams should escalate their response based on further evidence.

Even organizations not directly using Rust can be affected through third-party vendors, open-source builds, and shared CI infrastructure. Security Operations Centers (SOCs) should monitor network traffic and child processes under build tools, not just executable distribution.

headline_marked: [[Berkeley Law prohibits AI use]] in classes by default, citing cognitive skill development
headline: Berkeley Law prohibits AI use in classes by default, citing cognitive skill development
summary: The policy aims to ensure students develop critical thinking and ethical reasoning, essential for good lawyering, by forbidding AI for conceptualizing, drafting, or editing work for credit.
details: UC Berkeley School of Law has implemented a default policy prohibiting the use of artificial intelligence in most classes. This move is intended to ensure students develop fundamental cognitive skills necessary for effective legal practice.

The policy specifically bans AI for conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit. It also prohibits AI use for any purpose in exam situations and uploading course materials to generative AI systems.

Instructors retain the discretion to deviate from this default rule, particularly for courses designed to teach AI fluency. However, any authorized AI use must be disclosed by students and approved in writing by the instructor.

The school emphasizes that thinking remains paramount for quality legal education and good lawyering. The policy aims to equip students with the ability to master primary texts, apply legal reasoning, and independently develop creative solutions.

Students are responsible for the accuracy of their research, even when using AI for limited purposes like identifying sources. The policy warns that citations to non-existent sources will raise a presumption of prohibited AI use.
caption:
Future lawyers at Berkeley Law will develop critical skills without AI assistance. The school has implemented a default ban on generative AI for most coursework.
